tasks: Explain why the universal nature of the genetic code is evidence for a single common ancestor of all life.
Identify structurally conserved features across kingdoms that support ancestral links.

lectures.title: Population Genetics
lectures.description: Deconstructs genetic evolution in populations, quantitative Hardy-Weinberg modeling, genetic drift, gene flow, and patterns of selection.

sessions.title: Allele Frequencies
sessions.description: Define the genetic structure of a population by tracking gene pools and calculating allele and genotype frequencies.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by shifting our focus from the individual organism to the population as a whole. On the whiteboard, draw a large circle representing a geographic boundary, housing a group of interbreeding individuals of the same species. Inside this circle, write down various combinations of alleles (like AA, Aa, and aa) to visually establish the concept of a 'gene pool'—the sum total of all alleles for all genes in a population. It is vital to emphasize to students that while individual organisms possess static genotypes that do not change during their lifetime, it is the population's gene pool that evolves over time. This distinction is the core foundation of population genetics, framing evolution not as a magical transformation of an individual, but as a statistical shift in the genetic makeup of a group across generations.

Next, we transition to quantifying this gene pool by defining allele frequencies and distinguishing them from genotype frequencies. Use a simple, concrete whiteboard model: a population of 50 diploid individuals. Write down a hypothetical count, such as 30 homozygous dominant (AA), 15 heterozygous (Aa), and 5 homozygous recessive (aa) individuals. Ask the students: 'If each individual has two alleles for this gene, how many total alleles are in our gene pool?' Guide them to the answer of 100 alleles. From here, manually count the 'A' alleles (60 from the AA group plus 15 from the Aa group, totaling 75) and the 'a' alleles (15 from the Aa group plus 10 from the aa group, totaling 25). Define 'p' as the frequency of the dominant allele and 'q' as the frequency of the recessive allele, showing how 75/100 gives p = 0.75 and 25/100 gives q = 0.25, which naturally sums to 1. This step-by-step derivation ensures students grasp the mathematical reality before we introduce abstract formulas.

A frequent stumbling block for students is the tendency to confuse allele frequencies (p and q) with genotype frequencies (represented by the proportions of AA, Aa, and aa individuals). To prevent this, actively contrast the two on the board. Explain that genotype frequency represents the proportion of individuals carrying a specific pair of alleles, while allele frequency looks at the individual letters pooled together, regardless of how they are paired. Address another major misconception: the intuitive but incorrect belief that dominant alleles must naturally increase in frequency over time simply because they are 'dominant.' Explain that dominance refers only to how a gene is expressed phenotypically in a heterozygote, not its evolutionary fitness or its transmission rate.

Conclude the session with an interactive practice prompt. Have students calculate p and q from a new set of raw numbers—such as a population of 200 wildflowers with 120 red (RR), 60 pink (Rr), and 20 white (rr) individuals. Once they calculate the frequencies, ask them to predict what it would mean biologically if, five generations later, the frequency of 'r' dropped significantly. This discussion bridges raw math to biological reality, helping them realize that any sustained change in these numerical frequencies over time is the literal definition of microevolution in action.

tasks: Calculate allele frequencies (p and q) given a population's raw genotype counts.
Explain the biological significance of changing allele frequencies over successive generations.

sessions.title: Hardy–Weinberg Equilibrium
sessions.description: Master Hardy-Weinberg equations (p + q = 1, p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1) and analyze the five conditions required to maintain a non-evolving population.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by introducing the Hardy-Weinberg Principle as a 'null hypothesis' for evolution, a conceptual framework that is vital because it establishes what a population looks like when absolutely no evolutionary forces are acting upon it. This concept-first lecture style requires us to frame this not as a set of tedious math problems, but as a biological baseline—much like a control group in a laboratory experiment. By establishing this ideal state of genetic stasis, we can then identify and measure the exact evolutionary forces that cause real populations to deviate from it. We want to start with a blank whiteboard and write down the two primary equations: p + q = 1 and p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1. We must clearly define the variables, emphasizing that p represents the frequency of the dominant allele and q represents the frequency of the recessive allele in the gene pool, whereas the terms in the trinomial equation represent the frequencies of the actual diploid genotypes (homozygous dominant, heterozygous, and homozygous recessive, respectively).

To build a rock-solid derivation of these equations, we guide the teacher to use a visual probability grid (a Punnett-square-like representation of a population's random mating). Instead of crossing individuals, we are crossing the entire gene pool. If we randomly pull two alleles from a bucket containing a fraction 'p' of dominant alleles and 'q' of recessive alleles, the chance of getting two dominant alleles is p multiplied by p (p^2), the chance of getting two recessive alleles is q multiplied by q (q^2), and the chance of getting one of each is pq + qp, which simplifies to 2pq. This simple mathematical derivation unlocks the transition from individual allele frequencies to population-wide genotype frequencies. It is crucial to address a common learner misconception here: many students conflate the allele frequency (p or q) with the genotype frequency (p^2 or q^2). We prevent this by emphasizing that alleles exist in single gametes, while genotypes represent the paired genetic makeup of individual organisms.

Next, we introduce a concrete practice scenario to ground this math in a medical context. We present a population where a recessive genetic disorder has a frequency of 4%, or 0.04 (q^2 = 0.04). We walk through the logical steps of solving this: first, we must solve for the recessive allele frequency (q) by taking the square root of 0.04, which yields q = 0.2. From there, we use the linear equation p + q = 1 to find that p must equal 0.8. Finally, we calculate the frequency of heterozygous carriers using 2pq, which gives 2 * (0.8) * (0.2) = 0.32, or 32%. This practice is designed to reveal whether students can map the biological terms (such as 'carriers' or 'diseased individuals') directly to the correct mathematical variables. Teachers should explicitly point out the trap of trying to start calculations by taking the square root of the dominant phenotype frequency, explaining that dominant phenotypes actually bundle both homozygous dominant (p^2) and heterozygous (2pq) individuals together, making q^2 the only reliable starting point.

Finally, we transition from the mathematical model to the five physical conditions required for a population to remain in this non-evolving state. On the whiteboard, we list these conditions: an infinitely large population size (to prevent genetic drift), no migration or gene flow, no mutations, random mating, and no natural selection. We explain the biological 'why' behind each condition. For instance, if natural selection favors one phenotype, then certain alleles will be passed on more frequently, shifting p and q over time. By demonstrating how the violation of any single one of these five rules directly alters allele frequencies, we show that Hardy-Weinberg is not just a mathematical game, but a powerful diagnostic tool. If a real-world population's genotype frequencies do not match the predicted p^2, 2pq, and q^2 ratios, we know immediately that at least one of these five evolutionary forces is actively at work.

tasks: Solve for the expected frequency of heterozygous carriers in a population where the recessive disease frequency (q^2) is 0.04.
Identify the five evolutionary conditions that violate Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.

sessions.title: Genetic Drift and Gene Flow
sessions.description: Analyze random evolutionary changes, exploring genetic drift (founder and bottleneck effects) in small populations, and genetic exchange via gene flow.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by pivoting from the deterministic world of natural selection to the realm of random chance, emphasizing a concept-first public lecture style. The core objective is to dismantle the common student misconception that all evolutionary change is adaptive. On our physical or virtual whiteboard, draw a clear distinction: while natural selection actively filters traits based on fitness, genetic drift is completely blind to adaptation. It is a stochastic process where allele frequencies fluctuate purely due to random sampling errors, which has a disproportionately massive impact in small populations. To make this intuitive, we present the visual metaphor of a jar of colored marbles representing a gene pool. If we randomly draw only a tiny handful of marbles, we might entirely lose a color (an allele) by sheer chance, not because that color was 'unfit.' This visualization helps prevent the classic student error of thinking drift only happens when an environment changes.

Next, we transition to two classic scenarios of genetic drift: the bottleneck effect and the founder effect. On the whiteboard, sketch a hourglass bottle containing diverse colored beads representing a large parent population. Draw a narrow neck where only a few random beads slip through into a new glass. This physical bottleneck represents an environmental catastrophe—such as a wildfire or volcanic eruption—that decimates a population indiscriminately. Crucially, emphasize to students that the survivors do not survive because of 'good genes' but rather 'good luck.' Then, contrast this with the founder effect by drawing a small group of individuals migrating away from a large mainland to colonize a remote island. In both cases, the resulting gene pool is a random subset of the original, leading to a drastic loss of genetic diversity and a high risk of inbreeding depression.

We then introduce an active learning checkpoint to compare these mechanisms with positive natural selection. Ask students: 'If a population's genetic diversity plummets, how can we tell if it was caused by a selective sweep versus a population bottleneck?' Walk through the logic chain: natural selection leaves a signature of targeted adaptation, driving up the frequency of specific advantageous alleles while other parts of the genome remain diverse. A bottleneck, however, acts as a genomic-wide eraser, randomly driving random loci to fixation or extinction across the entire genome regardless of their utility. This comparison is vital for AP-level analysis, as it forces students to think about the genetic signature left behind by different evolutionary forces.

Finally, we introduce gene flow as the antidote to genetic drift. On the whiteboard, draw two distinct populations separated by a geographical barrier, such as a mountain range, with arrows representing individuals migrating and breeding between them. Explain that gene flow is the transfer of alleles into or out of a population due to the movement of fertile individuals or gametes. The critical concept here is homogenization: ongoing gene flow acts like a biological glue that keeps adjacent populations genetically similar, counteracting the diversifying effects of natural selection and the randomizing effects of genetic drift. If gene flow is cut off, these populations will drift apart genetically, setting the stage for speciation. Conclude by summarizing how drift creates random divergence, while flow fosters genetic uniformity across populations.

tasks: Compare the genetic outcomes of a bottleneck effect to positive natural selection.
Explain how gene flow can homogenize allele frequencies between adjacent populations.

sessions.title: Selection in Populations
sessions.description: Distinguish among directional, stabilizing, and disruptive selection patterns, using graphical representations of phenotypic shifts.
sessions.sessionOutline:
To begin this whiteboard-driven session, we establish a baseline conceptual understanding of how phenotypic variation is distributed in natural populations. Using the public-lecture, concept-first approach, the instructor will draw a standard bell-shaped curve representing a quantitative trait—such as birth weight in mammals or beak size in a seed-eating bird population. We start by explaining that natural selection does not just select 'for' or 'against' a single trait in isolation; it dynamically shifts entire distributions of phenotypes based on ecological pressures. The x-axis is labeled as the range of the phenotypic trait (from one extreme to another), and the y-axis represents the number of individuals exhibiting that trait. This initial drawing helps students visualize that most individuals hover around an average value, while fewer occupy the extreme ends. This foundation is crucial because all three selection patterns are relative modifications of this original curve.

Next, the instructor introduces the first scenario: Stabilizing Selection. This is illustrated by overlaying a new curve over the original bell curve. We show the distribution narrowing, with the peak rising higher in the center while both extreme tails shrink. To make this concept intuitive, we use the classic example of human birth weight or egg clutch size in birds: laying too few eggs leads to low reproductive success, while laying too many eggs results in malnourished chicks. The underlying logic here is that the environment is stable, and the average phenotype is already highly optimized. A common learner misconception is that stabilizing selection reduces genetic variation entirely to zero; the instructor must explicitly clarify that while it reduces phenotypic variance, genetic recombination and mutation continuously replenish variation, maintaining a dynamic balance.

We then shift the environmental context to introduce Directional Selection. The instructor draws an arrow pointing from the original peak toward one of the extremes, showing the entire bell curve shifting left or right. This occurs when a sustained environmental change favors individuals at one end of the phenotypic spectrum. For example, as trees darken due to industrial soot, lighter moths become targets for predators, shifting the population's color distribution toward the darker phenotype. The instructor points out that the peak itself moves, which unlocks the understanding that evolution is a response to selective pressures that change over time. It is vital to emphasize that the population does not 'choose' to adapt; rather, the existing variations that happen to fit the new environment survive and reproduce at higher rates.

Finally, we explore Disruptive Selection, which is often the most conceptually challenging. The instructor draws a dip directly in the middle of the original curve, creating a bimodal, 'two-humped' distribution. This pattern arises when the intermediate phenotype is at a disadvantage, while both extreme phenotypes are favored. A classic scenario involves a bird species in an environment with only very hard seeds and very soft seeds, where medium-sized beaks are inefficient for both. This visual representation serves as a perfect transition to discuss how disruptive selection can act as a precursor to speciation. 

To consolidate these concepts, the instructor initiates an interactive whiteboard sketching exercise. Students are asked to predict and draw what happens to a population of insects with varying green-to-brown coloration when a sudden, permanent drought turns the green grasslands into dry, brown brush with patches of vibrant green moss. This prompt forces students to choose between directional and disruptive models based on the ecological description, testing their ability to link environmental changes to phenotypic shifts. The session wraps up by reinforcing that while natural selection shapes these curves, the rate of environmental change dictates whether a population successfully adapts, goes extinct, or splits into diverging lineages.

tasks: Sketch phenotypic curves showing the shifts caused by stabilizing selection versus disruptive selection.
Predict which selection pattern is favored during rapid, radical environmental alterations.

lectures.title: Speciation and Evolutionary Relationships
lectures.description: Explores how new species arise and go extinct, and teaches students to read, build, and analyze phylogenetic trees.

sessions.title: Speciation
sessions.description: Study speciation pathways (allopatric, sympatric) and prezygotic/postzygotic reproductive isolation mechanisms.
sessions.sessionOutline:
To begin our deep dive into speciation, we establish the fundamental concept of what a species actually is under the biological species concept. Rather than relying on appearance, which can be highly misleading, we define a species as a group of populations whose members have the potential to interbreed in nature and produce viable, fertile offspring. The teacher should sketch two overlapping circles on the whiteboard representing gene pools, emphasizing that gene flow holds these populations together. When gene flow is interrupted, genetic divergence begins. This framing sets the stage for our exploration of isolation mechanisms, illustrating that speciation is not an overnight event but a gradual splintering of shared genetics.

Next, we transition to reproductive isolation mechanisms, dividing them into prezygotic and postzygotic barriers. On the whiteboard, draw a chronological timeline of a fertilization event: Pre-fertilization (Prezygotic) and Post-fertilization (Postzygotic). For prezygotic barriers, detail temporal isolation using the example of wood frogs and leopard frogs that mate in different weeks of the spring, and behavioral isolation using distinct courtship rituals of blue-footed boobies. A common misconception students face here is confusing geographic isolation (a physical barrier) with habitat isolation (ecological niches within the same area). Correct this by showing how two species of garter snakes might live in the same region, but one lives in water while the other is terrestrial. Then, move to postzygotic barriers, using hybrid sterility (such as a mule) to illustrate that even if mating occurs, evolutionary dead ends prevent gene flow from resuming. This chronological breakdown helps students realize that barriers act as sequential checkpoints.

We then contrast the geographic contexts of these barriers by comparing allopatric and sympatric speciation. Use the whiteboard to draw a simple cartoon of a single, continuous population of beetles. Draw a physical canyon splitting them—this is allopatric speciation, driven by geographic barriers like mountain ranges or rivers. Then, erase the canyon and present a scenario where a subpopulation shifts to a new host plant within the exact same forest—this represents sympatric speciation. Emphasize that while allopatric speciation is intuitive, sympatric speciation is harder to achieve because individuals are still in physical contact, making reproductive isolation much more difficult to establish without strong selective pressures.

To highlight a dramatic and rapid mechanism of sympatric speciation, we introduce plant polyploidy. On the whiteboard, map out a nondisjunction event during meiosis where a diploid plant produces diploid gametes instead of haploid ones. When these self-fertilize, they create a tetraploid offspring. Explain how this new plant is instantly reproductively isolated from its parent generation because any backcrossing would yield triploid offspring, which are sterile due to uneven chromosome alignment during meiosis. This serves as an excellent concrete example of how speciation can happen in a single generation, shattering the student misconception that evolutionary change always requires millions of years.

To wrap up the session, introduce an interactive practice prompt on the board: present students with a scenario involving two populations of marine snails separated by the Isthmus of Panama versus a population of cichlid fish in a single lake specializing on different prey types. Ask students to categorize each scenario and predict which reproductive barriers will evolve first. This exercise is designed to test whether students can synthesize the geographic context (allopatric vs. sympatric) with the operational mechanisms of isolation, ensuring they can apply these conceptual frameworks to real-world biological systems.

tasks: Contrast prezygotic isolation mechanisms (e.g., temporal, behavioral) with postzygotic isolation mechanisms (e.g., hybrid sterility).
Identify situations that trigger rapid sympatric speciation (e.g., polyploidy in plants).

sessions.title: Extinction
sessions.description: Analyze historic rates of background and mass extinctions, exploring ecological niches made available after extinction events.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by distinguishing between the constant, low-level background extinction rate and the sudden, catastrophic spikes known as mass extinctions. To make this concept-first approach resonate, visually map out a continuous timeline on the whiteboard. Draw a steady, low baseline representing background extinction—the gradual loss of species due to localized competition, gradual climate changes, or natural successional dynamics. Contrast this baseline with five distinct, dramatic vertical spikes to represent the traditional 'Big Five' mass extinctions. Explain to students that background extinction is a normal, ongoing ecological process driven by local environmental shifts, whereas mass extinctions represent global disruptions that fundamentally alter the biosphere's composition within a geologically brief window.

Transition next to the specific environmental factors that precipitate rapid global mass extinctions. On the whiteboard, list and connect the primary drivers of these historical events: massive volcanic activity (such as the Siberian Traps during the Permian extinction), asteroid impacts (like the Chicxulub impact at the end of the Cretaceous), and rapid global climate shifts. It is vital to emphasize that the immediate cause of extinction is rarely the initial physical impact itself, but rather the cascading global consequences—such as prolonged dark winters from atmospheric dust blocking sunlight, acid rain, rapid ocean acidification, and sudden drops in global oxygen levels. This sequential chain of events helps students move beyond the simplistic misconception that 'a rock hit Earth and everything died instantly' to a more sophisticated, ecologically grounded understanding of systemic collapse.

Now, introduce the profound evolutionary consequence of mass extinctions: the vacancy of ecological niches and the subsequent phenomenon of adaptive radiation. On the whiteboard, draw a branching tree diagram starting from a few surviving lineages. Explain how the sudden removal of dominant competitor groups—such as the non-avian dinosaurs—leaves countless ecological roles completely empty. This ecological vacuum reduces competition for resources, allowing surviving, generalist species to rapidly diversify and adapt to fill these new roles. Address the common student misconception that survivors are 'superior' in an absolute evolutionary sense; clarify that survival during mass extinctions is often a matter of ecological luck and generalist flexibility rather than long-term adaptive perfection.

Conclude the session with a practical whiteboard walkthrough of fossil record evidence. Sketch a simplified representation of geological strata, showing a dense layer of diverse fossils, a distinct boundary layer containing ash or high iridium levels, and a subsequent layer showing a dramatic reduction in fossil diversity followed by a rapid branching of new, diverse forms. Walk through this visual model to show how scientists read the fossil record to identify both the extinction event and the subsequent adaptive radiation. Ask students to interpret this diagram to identify which surviving lineages went on to dominate the post-extinction landscape, cementing their understanding of how mass extinctions serve as powerful creative forces that reshape the entire tree of life.

tasks: Analyze environmental factors that precipitate rapid global mass extinctions.
Explain adaptive radiation using fossil record events following mass extinctions.

sessions.title: Phylogenetic Trees and Cladograms
sessions.description: Learn to interpret and construct phylogenetic trees and cladograms to model evolutionary lineage relationships.
sessions.sessionOutline:
To begin our exploration of phylogenetic trees and cladograms, we must shift the learner's thinking from linear chains of progression to branching patterns of common ancestry. In this session, our virtual whiteboard serves as the primary canvas. Start by drawing a simple tree with a single root branching into two lineages. Explain that the root represents the common ancestor, while the tips represent modern or descendant species. The crucial concept here is that time flows from the root to the tips, and each node—or branching point—signifies a speciation event. Prevent the common misconception that species on the left 'evolved into' species on the right. Instead, emphasize that they share a common ancestor at a specific point in time, and the proximity of this node dictates how closely related they are.

Once the basic topology is clear, introduce key terms: sister taxa, monophyletic clades, and shared derived characters. Use the whiteboard to circle a group consisting of an ancestor and all of its descendants, labeling this a monophyletic group or clade. Contrast this with paraphyletic groupings to show why clades are the gold standard of evolutionary classification. To introduce shared derived characters, write tick marks on specific branches of the tree, representing evolutionary novelties that arose in the ancestor of that group and were passed down. Address a major learner pitfall here: confusion between homologous traits (due to shared ancestry) and analogous traits (due to convergent evolution). Explain that cladograms must be constructed using homologous traits to reflect true genetic history.

Transition to a hands-on character matrix construction activity to solidify these concepts. Draw a simple binary table on the whiteboard listing several organisms (e.g., lancelet, lamprey, tuna, rabbit) against a set of traits (e.g., vertebral column, jaws, hair). Guide learners through the step-by-step logic of building a cladogram from this table, starting with the organism that has none of the derived characters—the outgroup. The outgroup serves as our baseline. As we find traits shared by more and more organisms, we build nested groups, placing tick marks for each derived character on the correct ancestral branches. This exercise reveals whether learners truly understand how shared characteristics translate into branching nodes, allowing the instructor to correct indexing errors in real-time before wrapping up with a synthesis on how trees are hypotheses waiting to be tested with molecular data.

tasks: Identify sister taxa, monophyletic clades, and shared derived characters on a given cladogram.
Construct a simple cladogram from a character table of presence/absence traits.

sessions.title: Molecular Evidence and Evolutionary Relationships
sessions.description: Incorporate biochemical molecular data (amino acid/nucleotide sequences) to evaluate and refine evolutionary hypotheses.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by transitioning from morphological traits to the molecular realm. Historically, biologists grouped organisms based on physical similarities—such as wing structure or bone arrangement. However, physical structures can be deeply misleading due to convergent evolution, where unrelated organisms develop similar traits under similar environmental pressures. This session introduces molecular evidence as the modern gold standard of evolutionary biology, helping students understand that comparing genetic and amino acid sequences reveals the most accurate historical blueprint of life on Earth.

To build this conceptual bridge, we will construct a visual scenario on the whiteboard comparing two hypothetical organisms that look identical physically but have vast genomic differences. This contrasting example immediately confronts the classic student misconception that looking alike equals being closely related. By writing out short, representative snippets of DNA or amino acid sequences side-by-side, we demonstrate that while anatomy can lie, the genetic code is a permanent, accumulating record of evolutionary changes.

Next, we will model how to calculate and interpret percent identity values from aligned sequences. Using the whiteboard, we will draw a simple comparative matrix of DNA sequences among three modern species and one ancestral species. We will guide students through identifying point mutations, insertions, and deletions, showing how to count identical bases to determine percent identity. The core concept here is that a higher percentage of shared sequence identities correlates directly with a more recent common ancestor. We will call out a common trap: students often assume that long sequences are automatically more related, so we must emphasize that it is the percentage of alignment match, not the absolute length, that indicates evolutionary proximity.

To solidify these concepts, we will walk through a practice prompt where students evaluate raw sequence data to resolve a disputed node on a phylogenetic tree. This interactive challenge forces students to choose between a morphological hypothesis and a molecular hypothesis. In doing so, they practice articulating *why* molecular homology is more robust—namely, because it offers an immense, quantifiable data set (millions of base pairs) compared to a handful of subjective physical traits, and because it filters out the noise of convergent evolution. We conclude with a summary of how these molecular trees are continuously refined as genomic sequencing technology advances, reminding students that science is an iterative process of testing hypotheses with the best available data.

tasks: Determine the closest relative of a species using DNA sequence percent identity values.
Explain why molecular homology is preferred over morphological homology when constructing robust phylogenetic trees.

projects.stage_description: Construct a dynamic spreadsheet or script that models natural selection, genetic drift, and gene flow across multiple generations. You will test how violating Hardy-Weinberg assumptions shifts allele and genotype frequencies over time.
projects.deliverable_increment: Chapter 4 of the portfolio, including generation-by-generation allele frequency plots, selection coefficient impact tables, and a formal scientific hypothesis test of microevolutionary change.

exams.title: Unit 5 Examination: Natural Selection and Evolution
exams.goal: Verify the student's mastery of natural selection theory, Hardy-Weinberg mathematical modeling, speciation mechanics, phylogenetic tree interpretation, and molecular evolution.
sections: Comprehensive review of selection models, Hardy-Weinberg calculations, speciation pathways, and phylogenetic reconstructions.
successCriteria: Correctly solve and interpret Hardy-Weinberg mathematical scenarios.
Deconstruct speciation events into specific isolation mechanisms.
Correctly interpret and draw evolutionary inferences from phylogenetic trees and cladograms.

units.title: Ecology
units.description: Explores levels of ecological organization, population growth dynamics, community interactions, biodiversity, and ecosystem energy flows.

lectures.title: Population Ecology
lectures.description: Investigates population dynamics, modeling growth models, environmental carrying capacities, and life-history strategies.

sessions.title: Levels of Ecological Organization
sessions.description: Outline levels of ecological organization: organism, population, community, ecosystem, biome, and biosphere.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome students to the start of Unit 6: Ecology. We begin our ecological journey by establishing a framework for how biologists organize life on a grand scale. Many students struggle with ecology because they view it as a loose collection of nature facts rather than a highly structured, hierarchical science. Today, we will construct a visual ladder of ecological organization on the whiteboard, starting from a single individual and scaling all the way up to the global biosphere. The goal is to help students see that each step up this ladder introduces new properties and interactions that cannot be understood by looking at the individual components alone.

Let's start our whiteboard drawing with a single, isolated organism—for example, a lone sea otter floating in a kelp forest. At the individual organism level, a biologist's focus is on physiology, behavior, and how that specific creature survives and reproduces in its environment. But organisms do not live in vacuums. Draw a circle around that otter and add several other sea otters of the same species living in that same defined area. This brings us to our second level: the population. A population is defined as a group of individuals of the same species living in the same general area at the exact same time. The distinction is crucial because members of a population can interbreed and compete for the exact same resources. Emphasize to the class that natural selection acts on the individual organism, but evolution is measured at the population level over generations.

Now, expand the visual circle on the whiteboard. Draw kelp stalks, sea urchins, crabs, and predatory killer whales alongside our sea otters. This brings us to the community level. Ask the students: what changed when we added these other organisms? They will recognize that we are no longer looking at just one species, but rather all the biotic—or living—components in this ecosystem. Define a community as an assemblage of different populations of various species interacting with one another. A common student misconception here is confusing a population with a community; caution them that if they are discussing interactions *between* different species (like predation, competition, or mutualism), they have transitioned from population ecology to community ecology.

To move to the next level, we must introduce the abiotic factors. On the whiteboard, draw waves representing water currents, sunlight penetrating the ocean surface, and dissolved oxygen molecules. We have now arrived at the ecosystem level. An ecosystem includes all the biotic components (the community) in a given area, interacting with all the abiotic components (the non-living, physical, and chemical elements). Explicitly list out major abiotic factors like temperature, sunlight, soil chemistry, water availability, and salinity. Explain that these abiotic factors act as natural sieves or environmental filters, dictating exactly where organisms can survive and where they cannot. If water temperatures rise too high or nutrients drop, the kelp cannot survive, which collapses the food web for the otters and urchins.

Conclude the whiteboard visualization by zooming out to the global scale. Group similar ecosystems with similar climates and vegetation patterns into biomes, such as the temperate broadleaf forest or tundra. Finally, wrap all of Earth's biomes together into the biosphere, which encompasses every region of our planet where life exists, from deep ocean trenches to the high atmosphere.

To consolidate this understanding, guide the students through a quick practice exercise. Present them with a scenario: 'A scientist is studying how a sudden drought affects the reproductive rate of wild lupine flowers, and how that in turn alters the abundance of the local butterfly species that feed on them.' Ask the class to identify which level of ecological organization this study represents (community) and to categorize the drought as a biotic or abiotic factor (abiotic). This practice ensures students can successfully distinguish between populations and communities, while immediately applying the critical difference between biotic interactions and abiotic environmental constraints.

tasks: Define population and community within an ecological context.
Distinguish abiotic factors from biotic factors that dictate organismal distribution.

sessions.title: Population Growth
sessions.description: Analyze mathematical models of population growth, comparing exponential and logistic growth functions.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by establishing a clear conceptual foundation for how biological populations change in size over time. The transition from individual survival to collective population dynamics is driven by birth and death rates. Introduce the primary variable, $N$, representing total population size, and explain that the fundamental change in a population ($dN/dt$) over an instantaneous moment in time is dictated by the births minus the deaths. To make this intuitive, we define the per capita birth rate ($b$) and death rate ($d$)—essentially, the average number of offspring produced and deaths occurring per individual in a set time frame. By subtracting death rate from birth rate ($b - d$), we derive $r$, the intrinsic per capita growth rate. We want to emphasize to students that $r$ is a rate of change per individual, meaning a positive $r$ means the population is expanding, a negative $r$ means it is shrinking, and an $r$ of zero represents a stable, non-changing population. Instructors should walk through a simple calculation on the whiteboard using easy-to-follow integers before introducing algebraic formulas to avoid math anxiety.

Once the algebraic foundation of $r$ is secure, we transition to the whiteboard to map out the first major mathematical growth model: exponential growth, represented by the equation $dN/dt = rN$. We visualize this as a J-shaped curve, where the population size ($N$) is plotted on the y-axis against time ($t$) on the x-axis. Here, the instructor should highlight a common pitfall: students often mistake a low initial slope on the J-curve as a low rate of growth. We must explicitly point out that even though the growth rate $r$ remains completely constant, the absolute number of individuals added per unit of time ($dN/dt$) accelerates dramatically simply because the pool of reproducing individuals ($N$) is multiplying. To solidify this concept, run a quick thought experiment on the board showing how a population of 10 with an $r$ of 0.5 adds only 5 individuals, whereas a population of 1,000 with the same $r$ adds 500 individuals in the same time frame.

Next, we introduce a major biological reality check: resources are not infinite. This brings us to the logistic growth model, which modifies our exponential equation by introducing the concept of carrying capacity ($K$). We write out the full logistic equation, $dN/dt = rN((K - N)/K)$, and dissect the math step-by-step. The key here is to explain the term $((K - N)/K)$ as a 'feedback modifier' or the fraction of available resources remaining in the environment. When $N$ is very small, this term is close to 1, meaning the population grows almost exponentially. As $N$ approaches $K$, the term approaches 0, causing the overall growth rate to flatline and creating the characteristic S-shaped (sigmoid) curve on our whiteboard plot.

To ensure active cognitive engagement, lead the class through a sketching exercise on the board where students predict what happens to the slope of the curve at three distinct phases: when $N$ is much smaller than $K$, when $N$ is exactly half of $K$ (the inflection point of maximum growth rate), and when $N$ exceeds $K$ (where the growth rate becomes negative, representing overshoot and subsequent dieback). This exercise reveals whether students truly grasp the relationship between the algebraic terms and the physical shape of the graph, preparing them to confidently interpret similar diagrams on rigorous assessments.

tasks: Calculate the per capita growth rate (r) of a population using raw birth and death rate values.
Sketch population size (N) over time (t) for both exponential and logistic growth curves.

sessions.title: Carrying Capacity
sessions.description: Examine carrying capacity (K) limits, exploring density-dependent and density-independent factors that constrain population size.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session on the physical whiteboard by sketching a standard logistic growth curve, pointing out the plateau phase where population size levels off. Introduce the concept of Carrying Capacity, designated as 'K', not as a rigid, immutable ceiling, but as a dynamic, fluctuating equilibrium. This distinction is crucial because students frequently misinterpret carrying capacity as a physical barrier that a population can never cross, rather than a shifting balance between the biotic potential of a species and the environmental resistance of its habitat. Explain that K represents the maximum population size that a specific environment can sustainably support over time without degrading the resource base.

Transition into dissecting the biological mechanisms that regulate this equilibrium, starting with density-dependent factors. Draw a feedback loop on the board to illustrate how these factors scale in intensity alongside population density. Use the physical space of the whiteboard to map out two primary regulators: resource depletion and disease. Explain the step-by-step logic chain where a rising population density reduces the per capita availability of food, nesting sites, or clean water. This starvation or lack of breeding territory directly drives down the birth rate while elevating the death rate, slowing growth as N approaches K. For disease, illustrate how close physical proximity in crowded populations acts as a transmission superhighway, allowing pathogens to spread rapidly and causing mortality rates to spike only when density is high.

Contrast this immediately by drawing a sudden, vertical drop in the population curve to introduce density-independent factors. Explain that these events, such as natural disasters, extreme weather anomalies, or wildfires, decimate populations regardless of how sparse or dense they are. A frost kills the same percentage of tomato plants in a field whether there are ten or ten thousand. Ensure students understand that while density-dependent factors stabilize a population around K via negative feedback, density-independent factors act as external shocks that temporarily destabilize the system without respect to the population's current size.

Conclude with an active learning challenge on the whiteboard to consolidate these concepts and pre-empt common analytical errors. Ask the students to predict and draw two distinct scenarios: one where a volcanic eruption temporarily reduces a forest population but leaves the soil fertile, and another where human development permanently fragments the forest habitat. This exercise forces students to visually grapple with the difference between a temporary drop in population size (N) due to a density-independent disaster versus a permanent downward shift in the environmental carrying capacity (K) itself. By physically drawing these distinct trajectories, learners solidify their conceptual model of how environmental shifts alter the mathematical dynamics of population ecology.

tasks: Explain how resource depletion and disease act as density-dependent regulators.
Predict the long-term impact on a population curve when a density-independent factor (e.g., natural disaster) occurs.

sessions.title: Life-History Strategies
sessions.description: Deconstruct r-selection and K-selection reproductive strategies, analyzing survivorship curves (Types I, II, III).
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome back, students. Today we are bridging the quantitative aspects of population growth with the ecological realities of life-history strategies and survivorship curves. Because this is a concept-first public lecture style, we will rely on intuitive biological trade-offs, focusing on how different species allocate their limited energy toward growth, survival, and reproduction. On our whiteboard, we will sketch a conceptual spectrum. On one far end, write 'r-selection' (think 'rate' of growth), and on the other far end, write 'K-selection' (think carrying capacity 'K'). This spectrum is a fundamental evolutionary framework for understanding how organisms navigate resource limitations and environmental stability.

Let's start on the left side of our whiteboard with r-selected species. These organisms evolved in highly unstable or unpredictable environments where sudden disasters or seasonal changes dictate population size rather than competition. Because these populations rarely hit their carrying capacity limits, evolutionary pressure favors rapid reproduction. On the whiteboard, list the hallmark traits of an r-strategist: small body size, rapid development, early sexual maturity, and most importantly, producing a massive number of offspring with minimal to zero parental investment. Classic examples include dandelions, mosquitoes, and bacteria. The core strategy here is a numbers game: throw enough offspring into the world, and by sheer probability, a few will survive to pass on their genes. A common student misconception is that r-selected species are 'evolutionarily unsuccessful' because so many of their offspring die. Correct this by explaining that in a chaotic environment, investing all energy into a single, high-maintenance offspring is a massive evolutionary gamble that usually results in zero survival. Diversity and high reproductive output are successful adaptations for these specific niches.

Now, let's pivot to the right side of the whiteboard to examine K-selected species. These organisms thrive in stable, predictable environments that are consistently near carrying capacity (K). Because resources are limited, competition is intense, and quality of offspring matters far more than quantity. On the whiteboard, contrast this by listing K-selected traits: large body size, slow development, late maturity, and substantial parental care invested in a very small number of offspring. Examples include elephants, humans, and oak trees. These parents spend immense energy nurturing their offspring to ensure they are robust enough to compete effectively in a crowded, high-density environment. Point out that a common trap is thinking of organisms as strictly one or the other. In reality, life-history strategies exist on a continuous spectrum. For instance, sea turtles lay hundreds of eggs with no parental care (r-selected trait), yet they live for decades and have high adult survival rates (K-selected trait).

To visualize how these reproductive strategies play out over time, we will draw a set of axes on the whiteboard: the Y-axis representing 'Percent of survivors (logarithmic scale)' from 0 to 100%, and the X-axis representing 'Percent of maximum life span' from 0 to 100%. This is the standard Survivorship Curve graph. Draw three distinct lines. The first is Type I: a flat line that drops precipitously only at the end of the life span. This curve represents K-selected species, like humans, who have high survival rates throughout early and middle life because of intense parental protection, followed by steep mortality in old age.

Next, draw a diagonal, straight line downward from the top-left to the bottom-right corner. This represents a Type II survivorship curve. Here, organisms experience a constant rate of mortality throughout their entire life span. The probability of dying is the same at age one as it is at age ten, often due to consistent environmental pressures like predation or disease. Classic examples include songbirds, hydras, and many small rodents. Finally, draw a deep, sweeping curve that drops sharply right at the beginning and then flattens out near the bottom. This is the Type III curve, characteristic of r-selected species. These organisms experience massive infant mortality, but the lucky few that survive the initial gauntlet live on to reach a ripe old age.

Let's integrate this with an interactive practice scenario. Ask the students to imagine a newly formed volcanic island with empty niches, and a mature, dense rainforest. Have them predict which ecological strategy will dominate each environment and why. This exercise forces students to connect environmental stability to reproductive trade-offs, demonstrating that natural selection designs populations to balance their energy budget between current survival and future generations.

tasks: Classify organisms into r or K-selection strategies based on parental care, offspring size, and environment stability.
Analyze a survivorship curve graph, categorizing the mortality risk profiles of the plotted organisms.

lectures.title: Communities and Biodiversity
lectures.description: Explores how interacting populations form communities, the competitive dynamics of ecological niches, succession phases, and the importance of biodiversity.

sessions.title: Community Interactions
sessions.description: Investigate interspecific interactions, including competition, predation, herbivory, parasitism, mutualism, and commensalism.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome students to this session on community ecology. Begin the lecture by using a simple hook to ground the concept of ecological communities: ask students to imagine a forest not just as a collection of trees, but as an incredibly dense, invisible web of relationships where every organism is acting as a force upon another. Explain that while populations consist of a single species, communities are defined by the interactions between different species occupying the same area at the same time. The goal of today's lesson is to classify and analyze these relationships—collectively known as interspecific interactions—and understand how they shape the stability and structure of ecosystems. Use the concept-first approach to introduce symbols (+, -, 0) to represent the net effect on the fitness of each participant. This simple shorthand allows us to categorize complex biological phenomena systematically. 

Start the whiteboard breakdown by setting up a matrix of interactions. Begin with negative-impact interactions, specifically competition (-/-) and predation (+/-). When drawing out competition on the whiteboard, point out a common student misconception: many believe competition always involves physical fighting. Clarify that competition is more often indirect, such as two plant species struggling to absorb the same pool of soil nitrogen, where both species ultimately expend extra energy and suffer a reduction in potential growth. Next, transition to exploitation interactions like predation and herbivory. Illustrate how predation drives evolutionary arms races, using the visual analogy of a balance scale where prey defenses (like chemical toxins or camouflage) and predator offenses (like keen senses or claws) are constantly countering each other. Emphasize that herbivory is also a (+/-) relationship, as plants expend metabolic energy to produce secondary metabolites to deter herbivores.

Now, shift the whiteboard focus to symbiotic and facilitative interactions, starting with parasitism (+/-), then moving to mutualism (+/+) and commensalism (+/0). Take time to dive into mutualism using a real-world example, such as the relationship between mycorrhizal fungi and plant roots, or acacia ants and acacia trees. Guide the students to analyze this through a cost-benefit lens. Explain that mutualism is not 'cooperative harmony' but rather mutual exploitation where the benefit of the interaction exceeds the cost for both parties. For example, the tree spends energy producing nectar for the ants, but the protection from herbivores is worth the metabolic cost. Address commensalism (+/0) carefully, noting that true commensalism is rare in nature because it is incredibly difficult to prove that one organism is completely unaffected (0) by the presence of another.

Introduce the first active learning practice by presenting the classic predator-prey removal scenario. Ask the students to predict what would happen if a top predator, such as a sea star in an intertidal community or a wolf in a forest, is completely removed. Use the whiteboard to trace the cascading effects, showing how the absence of a predator allows a dominant competitor prey species to monopolize resources and inadvertently drive other prey species to local extinction. This introduces the concept of a keystone species and demonstrates that predation, counterintuitively, often preserves community diversity. Conclude by having students practice mapping out the energy trade-offs of a mutualistic relationship on their own, ensuring they understand that these interactions are dynamic balance sheets rather than static partnerships.

tasks: Analyze a mutualistic interaction, detailing the cost/benefit balance for both involved species.
Predict the outcome of removing a predator from a community of prey species.

sessions.title: Ecological Niches
sessions.description: Deconstruct the niche concept, comparing fundamental versus realized niches, resource partitioning, and competitive exclusion.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by introducing the core concept of an ecological niche, moving away from the common misconception that a niche is simply a physical place or habitat. Instead, we frame the niche as a multidimensional hypervolume—an abstract space representing all the physical, chemical, and biological factors a species needs to survive, grow, and reproduce. To make this intuitive, we draw a simple coordinate system on the board, plotting one dimension like temperature tolerance, and then adding a second dimension like food size, demonstrating how these overlapping requirements define a species' ecological role.

Next, we introduce the crucial distinction between a fundamental niche and a realized niche. The fundamental niche is the full potential range of conditions and resources a species could theoretically exploit in the complete absence of competition or limiting biotic interactions. We illustrate this on the whiteboard as a large, ideal circle representing maximum physiological tolerance. We then introduce a competing species into the ecosystem, showing how resource overlap forces our target species to contract its actual footprint. This restricted area is the realized niche—the actual set of conditions the species occupies in the real, messy world. A common pitfall for students is thinking the realized niche is somehow 'better' adapted; we must emphasize that the realized niche is a compromise forced by biotic pressure, representing survival under constraint.

This leads directly to Gause’s Principle of Competitive Exclusion. We explain the logical chain: if two species have identical niches, they cannot coexist indefinitely because one will inevitably be slightly more efficient at acquiring resources, driving the other to local extinction. We write this rule clearly on the board to anchor the lecture. To prevent a fatalistic view of ecology, we ask a rhetorical question: if exclusion is inevitable, why is nature so diverse? This introduces resource partitioning as the evolutionary escape hatch. Over time, natural selection favors individuals that minimize niche overlap, leading species to divide resources by space, time, or specific prey size.

Finally, we transition to character displacement as the physical, evolutionary evidence of past competition. When two competing species live apart (allopatry), their physical traits like beak size or body length may look nearly identical because they face similar solitary selective pressures. However, when they live together (sympatry), natural selection drives their physical traits apart to facilitate resource partitioning. On the whiteboard, we plot two overlapping bell curves representing trait distribution in isolation, and then draw them shifting away from each other in cohabitation. We close the session with a practice prompt asking students to analyze a hypothetical scenario involving two finch species, prompting them to predict how beak morphology shifts when they colonize the same island, which exposes whether they truly grasp how evolutionary traits respond to ecological competition.

tasks: Distinguish between a species' fundamental niche and realized niche in the presence of competitors.
Explain how character displacement reduces competitive pressure between overlapping species.

sessions.title: Ecological Succession
sessions.description: Study ecosystem development, detailing the changes and timelines of primary and secondary succession.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by visualizing a blank slate: a landscape completely devoid of life, organic soil, or history. This is the starting point of primary succession, and it is crucial to emphasize to learners that the defining characteristic here is the absolute absence of soil. Using a public, concept-first lecture style, we draw a harsh, rocky volcanic island newly emerged from the ocean, or a landscape scoured clean by a retreating glacier. The key biological question we present is: how does life establish itself when there is literally nothing to anchor to or draw nutrients from? This is where we introduce the pioneering heroes of primary succession: lichens and mosses. We describe how these organisms work in tandem with physical weathering to break down bare rock into microscopic mineral particles, which then mix with their own decaying organic matter to initiate the painfully slow process of soil formation.

Next, we contrast this slow, geological-scale process with secondary succession. We ask the class to imagine a vibrant forest suddenly swept by a wildfire, or an abandoned agricultural field. Here, the soil remains intact. We illustrate this on the whiteboard by drawing a rich, dark subterranean layer already packed with dormant seeds, root systems, and active microbes. Because the soil is already present, the recovery timeline is radically accelerated. Pioneer species here are not lichens, but fast-growing, sun-loving annual weeds and grasses that quickly carpet the barren ground. By juxtaposing these two starting conditions, we help students avoid the common misconception that 'pioneer species' is a fixed list of organisms; instead, we clarify that the identity of pioneers is entirely dependent on whether soil is present at time zero.

We then trace the predictable sequence of community changes as ecological succession progresses over time. As the pioneer species die and decompose, they enrich the soil, creating a deeper, more nutrient-rich substrate. This physical modification of the environment allows intermediate species—such as shrubs, fast-growing pines, and softwoods—to take root. These plants grow taller, eventually shading out the original sun-loving pioneers. This introduces a beautiful ecological irony: the very presence of early-colonizing species alters the environment in a way that makes it less favorable for their own offspring, but highly favorable for colonizing competitors. We map this transition on a whiteboard timeline, tracking how species richness and biomass rise steadily until the community reaches a relatively stable state, historically termed the climax community, dominated by slow-growing, shade-tolerant hardwood trees like oaks and maples.

To prevent students from viewing ecological succession as a rigid, one-way conveyor belt ending in a permanent 'climax' state, we shift our focus to the dynamic nature of disturbances. We present the Intermediate Disturbance Hypothesis. We ask students to consider what happens in a forest that never experiences a storm, fire, or tree-fall versus one that is constantly battered by destructive events. If disturbances are too frequent or severe, the community remains trapped in the pioneer phase with low species diversity. Conversely, if there are no disturbances, a few dominant competitors exclude all other species, also resulting in low diversity. It is at intermediate levels of disturbance—where occasional tree-falls or small fires open up light gaps in the canopy—that biodiversity peaks, allowing pioneers, intermediate species, and climax species to coexist in a complex mosaic. We conclude with an interactive practice scenario where students predict diversity outcomes in varying disturbance regimes, reinforcing how environmental instability actually serves as a vital engine for maintaining community diversity.

tasks: Contrast the starting conditions and pioneer species of primary succession with those of secondary succession.
Describe the role of disturbances in maintaining community diversity.

sessions.title: Biodiversity
sessions.description: Evaluate biological diversity at genetic, species, and ecosystem levels, calculating Simpson's Diversity Index.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by establishing a clear, multi-tiered definition of biodiversity, moving away from the simplistic view that it merely counts the number of species in an area. To set the stage, we introduce biodiversity across three distinct biological scales: genetic diversity (the variety of alleles within a single population), species diversity (the variety and relative abundance of different species in an ecological community), and ecosystem diversity (the range of different habitats and ecological processes across a landscape). We emphasize that genetic diversity is the ultimate fuel for evolutionary adaptation. If a pathogen or a sudden climate shift strikes a genetically uniform crop field, the entire population could be wiped out. In contrast, a genetically diverse population is highly resilient because a subset of individuals will likely possess alleles that confer resistance or tolerance to the new stressor. This connection to natural selection helps students see biodiversity not as a static ecological metric, but as an active, protective buffer against environmental change.

Next, we pivot to the quantitative evaluation of species diversity, which requires introducing two key components: species richness (the total number of different species present) and species evenness (how close in numbers each species in an environment is). To make this intuitive, we construct a virtual whiteboard comparison between two hypothetical forest communities. Forest A and Forest B both contain exactly four tree species and 100 total individual trees, meaning their species richness is identical. However, in Forest A, 97 trees belong to a single dominant species, while the other three species are represented by only one individual each. In Forest B, each of the four species has exactly 25 individuals. We ask students which forest feels more diverse, guiding them to realize that Forest B is far more balanced and resilient. This intuitive gap is where we introduce the mathematical tool designed to capture both richness and evenness simultaneously: Simpson's Diversity Index.

We present the standard AP Biology formula for Simpson's Diversity Index, written as D = 1 - sum of (n/N)^2, where 'n' represents the total number of organisms of a particular species, and 'N' represents the total number of organisms of all species. We walk through a step-by-step derivation of what this equation actually measures. The term (n/N) is the probability of randomly choosing an individual of a given species. Squaring it, (n/N)^2, gives the probability that two randomly selected individuals from the community will belong to that same species. By summing these squared probabilities across all species, we get the overall probability that any two randomly drawn organisms are of the identical species. Subtracting this sum from 1 yields the probability that two randomly chosen individuals will belong to different species. A higher value of D (closer to 1) signifies a highly diverse and balanced community, while a lower value (closer to 0) indicates a highly dominated, low-diversity community.

To solidify this mathematical intuition, we conduct a whiteboard practice calculation using the Forest A and Forest B data. Students run the calculations for both forests to observe how the unevenness of Forest A drives its D value extremely low, while the perfect evenness of Forest B pushes its D value close to 0.75. A common student misconception here is confusing the raw sum of squared probabilities (which decreases as diversity increases) with the final index value (1 minus the sum), leading to inverted conclusions. We explicitly address this by showing how the subtraction step is what aligns the index with our intuitive understanding of diversity. This practice reveals whether students can transition smoothly from biological concepts to quantitative reasoning and back again.

We conclude by connecting high biodiversity to ecosystem stability and resource dynamics. Diverse communities are generally more productive because different species utilize different niches, preventing empty niches that could easily be invaded by non-native species. We ask students to predict what would happen if a keystone species or a dominant producer were removed from both a low-diversity and a high-diversity community. Students should recognize that the high-diversity community has redundant pathways for energy flow and nutrient cycling, meaning other species can step in to fill the functional void, whereas the low-diversity community faces potential trophic cascades and ecological collapse. This final synthesis prepares students to apply both qualitative and quantitative reasoning to any ecology prompt on the AP exam.

tasks: Calculate Simpson's Diversity Index for two community data sets to determine species richness and evenness.
Explain why high genetic diversity within a population increases resilience against environmental changes.

lectures.title: Ecosystems and Environmental Change
lectures.description: Analyzes the thermodynamics of ecosystems, the flow of nutrients via biogeochemical cycles, and the impacts of human activities on ecological systems.

sessions.title: Energy Flow Through Ecosystems
sessions.description: Detail trophic structures, calculating energy transfer efficiency across primary producers, primary consumers, secondary consumers, and decomposers.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing the foundational physics governing all biological life: the laws of thermodynamics. Students often view ecosystems as self-sustaining loops, but we must immediately correct this misconception by emphasizing that while matter cycles, energy flows in a one-way path and is continuously lost as heat. We will start on the whiteboard by drawing a large, open system diagram. First, label the Sun as the ultimate, external source of high-quality energy. Show solar radiation entering the system, where a fraction is captured by primary producers (autotrophs) via photosynthesis. It is crucial here to distinguish between Gross Primary Productivity (GPP)—the total chemical energy captured—and Net Primary Productivity (NPP), which is GPP minus the energy the autotrophs consume for their own cellular respiration. To make this intuitive, we can use a financial analogy: GPP is a company's gross revenue, respiration is the cost of doing business, and NPP is the net profit that is actually available for saving or investment—or in this case, available for consumption by herbivores.

Next, we expand the diagram upward into a trophic pyramid, positioning primary producers at the base, followed by primary consumers (herbivores), secondary consumers (carnivores), and finally, tertiary consumers. We will write out the 10% ecological efficiency rule, showing that only about 10% of the energy stored as biomass in one trophic level is incorporated into the biomass of the next level. We must explicitly unpack where the other 90% goes to prevent the common student mistake of assuming it simply disappears. On the whiteboard, draw outward arrows from each level labeled as 'cellular respiration,' 'waste (feces),' and 'uneaten biomass,' all feeding into the decomposers (detritivores) like fungi and bacteria, which eventually release this energy as low-quality heat. Introduce a quick practice calculation on the board: if an ecosystem's NPP is 10,000 kJ/m²/year, ask students to estimate the net secondary productivity of the primary consumers, and then the secondary consumers. This mathematical check ensures they can apply the decimal shift of the 10% rule, while reinforcing that secondary productivity refers to the rate at which consumers convert organic material into their own new biomass.

Finally, we pivot to ecological pyramids of biomass, comparing terrestrial ecosystems with open-ocean ecosystems to address a profound conceptual paradox. On the left side of the board, draw a standard, upright pyramid of biomass typical of a grassland, where the dry weight of grasses vastly exceeds that of the herbivores and predators. On the right side, draw an inverted pyramid of biomass representing an oceanic ecosystem, where the phytoplankton biomass at any single moment is actually smaller than the biomass of the zooplankton feeding on them. We must guide students through the underlying logic here: why does this not violate the laws of thermodynamics? The key lies in the turnover rate. Phytoplankton have an incredibly high rate of reproduction and a short lifespan; they convert solar energy to chemical energy rapidly and are consumed almost immediately. Thus, while their standing crop biomass at any instant is small, their total productivity over time is massive enough to support a larger standing biomass of longer-lived zooplankton. This distinction between instantaneous biomass (a snapshot in time) and productivity (energy flow over time) is a frequent point of confusion on AP free-response questions, and illustrating it side-by-side prepares students to construct clear, thermodynamically sound explanations.

tasks: Calculate the estimated net secondary productivity of a trophic level given net primary productivity and a 10% transfer rule.
Explain why biomass pyramids are typically upright, whereas oceanic biomass pyramids can occasionally invert.

sessions.title: Biogeochemical Cycles
sessions.description: Trace water, carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus through biological, geological, and chemical reservoirs.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by establishing a fundamental contrast that grounds all biogeochemical cycles: while energy flows one-way through an ecosystem and eventually dissipates as heat, matter is strictly recycled. Draw a large, continuous loop on the whiteboard to represent this closed system of atoms. Explain that the same carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus atoms present during the age of the dinosaurs are still cycling through our biosphere today. Introduce the concept of 'reservoirs'—differentiating between biotic reservoirs (living organisms) and abiotic reservoirs (atmosphere, water, soil, and rocks). Emphasize that the movement between these reservoirs is driven by biological, geological, and chemical processes. This conceptual foundation helps students see these cycles not as a set of memorized diagrams, but as dynamic balancing acts of molecular exchange.

Transition to the carbon cycle by drawing two primary arrows on the board: one moving carbon from the atmosphere into living things, and one moving it back. Label these 'Photosynthesis' and 'Cellular Respiration.' Address a major student misconception here: many students mistakenly believe that plants only perform photosynthesis while animals only perform respiration. Clarify that plants do both, and both processes are essential for driving the short-term biological carbon cycle. Expand the diagram to include deeper, long-term abiotic reservoirs, such as deep-ocean sediments and fossil fuels buried underground. Explain how human activity, specifically the burning of fossil fuels and widespread deforestation, acts as a massive shortcut that bypasses geological timescales, dumping ancient locked-away carbon directly back into the atmospheric reservoir and disrupting global thermal dynamics.

Next, introduce the nitrogen cycle, framing it with a biological puzzle: nitrogen is an absolute requirement for building proteins and nucleic acids, and it makes up nearly eighty percent of our atmosphere, yet organisms cannot directly breathe it in or absorb it from the air. Draw the chemical structure of diatomic nitrogen ($N_2$) on the board, highlighting its exceptionally strong triple covalent bond. Explain that this bond is a locked vault that plants and animals cannot open. Introduce the biological 'locksmiths' of this cycle: nitrogen-fixing bacteria. Describe how these specialized prokaryotes, often living symbiotically in the root nodules of legumes or free in the soil, break this triple bond to convert atmospheric nitrogen into ammonium ($NH_4^+$), which plants can finally assimilate. Walk through the subsequent steps of nitrification (converting ammonium to nitrates) and denitrification (returning nitrogen to the atmosphere) on the whiteboard to illustrate how the loop closes.

Contrast the nitrogen and carbon cycles with the phosphorus cycle to highlight key structural differences. Draw a terrestrial landscape on the board, leaving the sky empty to visually emphasize that the phosphorus cycle lacks an atmospheric phase. Explain that phosphorus—essential for DNA backbones, cell membranes, and ATP—is primarily stored in sedimentary rock reservoirs. Detail how geological uplifting and subsequent weathering slowly release phosphate ions into the soil and water, where they are taken up by plants. Because this process relies on slow physical weathering rather than rapid biological or atmospheric transport, phosphorus is often the primary limiting nutrient in ecosystems, a concept crucial for understanding ecological growth and human-induced imbalances like eutrophication.

Conclude the session with an interactive whiteboard synthesis. Draw a scenario map depicting a agricultural field next to a body of water. Ask students to trace how human interventions, such as chemical fertilizer runoff containing excess nitrogen and phosphorus, bypass natural rate-limiting steps. Have them map out the chain of events from nutrient influx to bacterial blooms and eventual oxygen depletion (hypoxia). Guide them through the practice tasks, asking them to explain why an ecosystem would collapse if nitrogen-fixing bacteria were suddenly eliminated, and to predict the systemic effects of carbon cycle disruptions on global biomes. This synthesizes their conceptual understanding, preparing them to analyze complex ecological feedback loops on the AP exam.

tasks: Describe the critical role of nitrogen-fixing bacteria in transforming atmospheric nitrogen for biological assimilation.
Explain how carbon cycle disruption alters global atmospheric carbon dioxide reservoirs.

sessions.title: Ecosystem Responses to Disruption
sessions.description: Examine how ecosystems respond to changes, studying trophic cascades, introduction of invasive species, and habitat fragmentation.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by introducing the concept of ecosystem stability through a simple, intuitive analogy: a Jenga tower. In any ecological community, species are interconnected like blocks in a tower. While removing some blocks might cause only minor wobbles, removing others can cause the entire structure to collapse. This introduces the concept of the 'keystone species'—a term derived from the central stone in an arch that holds all other stones in place. On the whiteboard, draw a simple arch to visually anchor this terminology, emphasizing that a keystone species has an exceptionally large impact on its ecosystem relative to its abundance.

To explore the consequences of removing a keystone species, we map out a classic classic food web on the whiteboard: sea otters, sea urchins, and kelp forests. Walk students through the logic of a 'trophic cascade' by drawing arrows of interaction. Show how sea otters keep sea urchin populations in check, which allows kelp forests to thrive and provide habitats for dozens of other marine species. When we erase the sea otter from our diagram, we trace the resulting domino effect: urchin populations explode, they overgraze the kelp, and the entire habitat collapses into an 'urchin barren.' Address a common student misconception here: many believe that removing a predator only affects its direct prey. Use this visualization to prove that the effects cascade all the way down to primary producers and physically alter the ecosystem's architecture.

Next, we transition from removing a species to introducing a new one by exploring invasive species. Define an invasive species not just as a non-native organism, but as one that causes ecological or economic harm. On the whiteboard, draw two population growth curves side-by-side: a standard logistic growth curve showing a native species leveling off at its carrying capacity (K), and an exponential growth curve shooting rapidly upward. Ask students why native species level off while invasive species undergo explosive, exponential growth. Guide their intuition to realize that native species are constrained by evolutionary checks and balances—predators, specific diseases, and localized competitors. Invasive species, having evolved elsewhere, bypass these local limiting factors, essentially playing the game of survival with 'cheat codes.'

We round out our exploration of disruption by looking at habitat fragmentation. Draw a large, contiguous green square on the board representing a pristine forest, and then draw lines through it representing roads and suburban developments, dividing it into tiny isolated patches. Introduce the concept of 'edge effects.' Explain that the perimeter of a habitat has different microclimates (more wind, sunlight, and vulnerability to predators) than the interior core. By fragmenting the habitat, we drastically increase the ratio of edge-to-interior habitat, which selectively disadvantages deep-forest specialists while favoring generalist edge species. This visual layout helps students understand that biodiversity loss isn't just about losing total area, but about changing the structural geometry of the landscape.

To check for deep understanding, conclude with an interactive practice scenario. Present a food web containing a top predator, an herbivore, a disease-causing fungus, and a primary producer. Ask students to predict the ecological ripple effects if an invasive herbivore immune to the local fungus is introduced.
